parsed.explanation: The combined operative regime documents a criminal statute (Art. 489, 6 months–3 years) applied to trans gender expression, with wide police discretion, arbitrary arrests and 170 charges (2018); morality provisions (Art. 498) and gender-expression discrepancies supply additional de facto criminalisation. Police abuse is on the record: forced genital display (2024), handcuffing/filming and online posting of a cross-dresser's documents (2019). Outing is institutionalised — names publicised pre-trial — while no anti-discrimination law, no legal recognition, blocked LGBTIQ organisations and official hostility ('trash') leave no working remedy. Public identification carries significant violence risk; 21% societal acceptance and marches demanding punishment show hostile society aligned with hostile law. No execution pathway is documented, keeping this above the 0.15 tier.

entry_documents.exposure: Gender-expression discrepancies drive involuntary outing and de facto criminalisation; a cross-dresser's ID documents were photographed and posted online after a traffic stop (2019). No recorded treatment of foreign trans visitors' documents at entry.
entry_documents.interaction: Document/appearance mismatch → police suspicion → Art. 489/498 charge or public exposure; no shield for visitors using home passports.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Art. 489 enforced with wide police discretion and arbitrary arrests; applied to trans people for gender expression (Jan 2026 report). Prosecutions proceed on thin evidence; names publicised before trial. Custody conditions for trans detainees not documented.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: Stopping/stop-check → forced outing → morality or indecency charge; acquittals possible but slow and provoke public outcry.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: Subnational record shows incidents clustered in named cities with no national comparison; no facility-level (bathroom, ward) rules documented for visitors either way.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: National criminalisation and police practice operate uniformly across cities; locality neither mitigates nor adds documented exposure.

care_services.exposure: No gender-affirming healthcare framework; de facto prohibition on surgery; self-medication widespread. Emergency or routine care for an outed trans visitor is undocumented and unsafe to assume; no visitor shelter provision recorded.
care_services.interaction: Care-seeking while outed exposes the visitor to a system with no trans-specific provisions and a senior religious authority opposed to transition.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: State threat-framing: justice minister called homosexuals 'trash'; school curriculum teaches 'danger and depravity of unnatural acts'; books banned; LGBTIQ organisations blocked; top religious official opposes transition.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: International scrutiny (UNHCR-type SOGI resolution) exists but no domestic institutional protection documented.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Official hostility licenses police discretion and public hostility toward an outed visitor.

minors_guardians.exposure: A 2016 case saw two girls arrested after a relative's photograph, acquitted only after months amid public outcry — showing minors are not shielded. No family-travel provision documented; a travelling parent's outing risks custody and social fallout.
minors_guardians.protection: Acquittal in that case, though delayed and followed by public hostility.
minors_guardians.interaction: Minor's visibility or incident → police involvement → outing of parent as trans; no anti-discrimination protection.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: Public identification as LGBTIQ carries significant risk of violence/harassment; 2020 outing campaign with evictions and alleged suicide; Nov 2022 trans woman beaten (arrests made); police forced genital display (2024); filming/humiliation by officers; streets marched for punishment after 2007 conviction; only 21% find homosexuality acceptable.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Some perpetrators arrested (2022 beating; 2016 acquittal), showing partial accountability.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Societal hostility plus police participation in outing means calling police may worsen exposure.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: No anti-discrimination law, no legal gender recognition, LGBTIQ organisations blocked, prosecutions on thin evidence — no documented working remedy for a visitor. Unknowns: entry-document treatment, custody placement, current enforcement frequency (2018 charge figures only).
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Blocked civil society means the visitor lacks the local recourse that might otherwise offset hostile law.

anchor_checks.comparison: Similar in criminalisation applied at transit/document checks and illusory remedies, but Varnalia documents months of pretrial custody with guard beatings and reliance on coerced confessions; this dossier has no documented custodial violence pattern or capital provision, so it sits above 0.15-A.

Comparable: an identity/gender-expression statute enabling detention, police extortion/humiliation, hostile public. Lower than 0.25-A because that anchor documents courts overturning convictions and legal aid winning settlements, while here remedies are absent, organisations are blocked and names are publicised pre-trial.

Higher than 0.35-A. Vellandra's register excludes and humiliates but never threatens custody; this dossier documents a real imprisonment pathway (up to 3 years), arbitrary arrests, police abuse of the body and aligned societal hostility — materially more severe than exclusion alone.

Much higher. Kestrel Isles offers administrative refusal with written reasons, appeal desks and consular notification; this dossier's discovery pathway runs to criminal charge, public outing and police abuse with no documented remedy — a full tier or more apart.

parsed.synthesis: Law and society are aligned against the traveller: a criminal statute demonstrably used against gender expression, morality provisions supplying de facto criminalisation, police who personally participate in outing (filming, forced genital display, posting documents), and a public that marched for punishment and accepts homosexuality at 21%. Discovery is institutionalised — names publicised before trial — so discretion cannot be relied on. No offsetting machinery exists for a visitor: no anti-discrimination law, no recognition pathway, blocked LGBTIQ organisations, no trans-specific care. Some accountability appears (assailants arrested, one acquittal), preventing a lower score, but no documented remedy works for an outed trans visitor. Absence of execution or documented custodial torture keeps it out of the 0.10–0.15 band; the interlocking hostility with no recourse places it at the bottom of High Risk.
